title: Russell set for grid penalty at Sao Paulo Grand Prix
excerpt:
George Russell is set to take a grid penalty at the Sao Paulo Grand Prix due to an engine change, marking his second such penalty in the last four rounds.

Russell was forced to serve a significant penalty at the Singapore Grand Prix due to a range of unavoidable power unit component changes, having retired with a power unit failure one week earlier at the Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia.

The Briton had been expected to serve another penalty at some stage during the remainder of the season and that now looks set to happen at Interlagos, with the Mercedes driver discussing the decision to take it at this track in an Instagram Stories post shared by the team.

“I mean, we always had to take a grid penalty at some point between Singapore… obviously we took one in Singapore, but from Singapore until the end of the season,” Russell explained.

“We felt like this was a good place to take it. Lewis [Hamilton] had a big grid penalty here a number of years ago and did pretty well. Five places doesn’t seem that bad, and we’ll try and come back through.”

Hamilton was disqualified from Sprint Qualifying in Brazil back in 2021, forcing him to start the Sprint from the back of the field. He subsequently climbed through the field to fifth before winning Sunday’s Grand Prix from 10th, having taken another penalty.

With the change on Russell’s car reportedly being for a fresh Internal Combustion Engine (ICE), the British driver’s penalty looks set to be a five-place grid drop.

It comes one week on from a tough weekend in Mexico for Russell, with Team Principal Toto Wolff admitting that the 28-year-old had been “distraught” at the outcome.

title: Bearman doesn’t see Camara’s debut ‘as a shoot-out’
excerpt:
Haas’ Ollie Bearman believes that going up against another Ferrari junior in Rafael Camara doesn’t constitute “a shoot-out”, with the latter set to make his F1 debut on home soil at the Sao Paulo Grand Prix.

Camara had earned a full-time seat with the American squad for 2027, but with Haas’ confirmation that Esteban Ocon will not race for them again this year, the Brazilian’s introduction to the grid was brought forward.

Currently on course to win the F2 title, Camara is yet to drive a 2026 F1 challenger, having only run an old-spec Haas in a test that convinced Team Principal Ayao Komatsu of his raw speed a few months ago.

His first race weekend will therefore be a crucial one in terms of learning, which Bearman is hopeful will give him an idea of how their dynamic as team mates will play out in future seasons.

“I think this is a bit of a preview for next year,” he told the media in Brazil. “I don't see it as a shoot-out but of course it's good to have a team mate that's going to push you – that's what we want as drivers.

“We're competitive, we want to have somebody that's going to force us to level up and I think Rafa will do that, as Esteban did, as all of my team mates have done. I think the eyes are going to be on us but it's an exciting battle.

“For sure it will be a bit more pressure [on Camara] but I think the opportunity of having your first F1 race at home is pretty unique, not many people get that. Only the Australians get that.

“I don't know many people who got to do their first-ever F1 race at home. Of course the circumstances are challenging, but I think it's a great opportunity for him, and I'm really happy for him. To get an F1 debut is one of those key moments in life, so very nice.”

It’s not been the most successful triple header for Bearman, who has failed to finish the last two races and is acutely aware that Audi are now only four points behind Haas in the Teams’ Championship.

However, he also explained that his previous experiences at Interlagos – which included filling in as a last-minute substitute at Haas, similar to Camara’s situation – will help him pursue the best possible result for the team.

Bearman said: “Of course our goal as a team is to try and retain P7 in the Constructors'. Mexico was a challenging weekend for us, losing out on points the way we did, and for the rest of the season we just need to try and score as much as we can, as often as we can.

“This weekend is an opportunity, with the weather as well. It's definitely going to be a challenging one for everybody, especially with Rafa jumping in. But he'll be up to speed quickly I'm sure and let's see how the weather looks.

“Of course I had the opportunity to jump in two years ago where it was a very challenging event, a lot of rain on Sunday especially. But with that weather comes opportunities and I hope that we can make the most of them.

“It's funny how many coincidences there are, but it's nice to be the more experienced driver and I'm excited to see what changes to be honest.

“I feel like I was kind of working towards leading the team and I knew that was a very important role. I don't think much will suddenly change this weekend and the main goal is of course to score points – that doesn't change.”

title: Which rookies are getting FP1 outings in Brazil?
excerpt:
Six F1 teams will field rookie drivers during Friday’s opening practice session for the Sao Paulo Grand Prix, with several familiar faces returning to the track just one week after their outings in Mexico City.

As per the 2026 regulations, every full-time racer must make way for a rookie, defined as someone who has started no more than two Grands Prix, in two practice sessions across the season. The newcomers will have one hour behind the wheel before handing their cars back for FP2, while Rafael Camara is preparing for a different challenge as he makes his full F1 debut for Haas.

But who exactly will be out on track? Here’s an overview of the six drivers taking part in FP1, plus the Brazilian youngster making his first Grand Prix appearance…

Leonardo Fornaroli – McLaren

Leonardo Fornaroli will return to the wheel of McLaren’s MCL40 for the second consecutive weekend after making his third FP1 appearance of the season in Mexico City.

The reigning F2 champion joined McLaren’s Driver Development Programme after securing back-to-back titles in F3 and F2, and has been building his experience through private tests and practice sessions. His preparations included a recent Testing of Previous Cars (TPC) outing at Circuit Paul Ricard, where he completed almost 350 kilometres before finishing P17 in Mexico City’s FP1 session.

After replacing Lando Norris last time out, the 21-year-old will now step into Oscar Piastri’s car at Interlagos, completing McLaren’s mandatory rookie practice allocation.

Dino Beganovic – Ferrari

Ferrari opted not to field a newcomer in the rookie-filled FP1 session in Mexico City, but Dino Beganovic will return to the SF-26 for another appearance with the Scuderia.

A member of the Ferrari Driver Academy since 2020, the 22-year-old Swede has already completed two FP1 outings this year, in Austria and Barcelona. Beganovic impressed during these appearances, finishing eighth in Barcelona and ninth in Austria, where he completed 26 laps.

Currently competing in F2 with DAMS, he will once again replace Charles Leclerc as Ferrari look to gather valuable data during Friday’s opening practice session.

Luke Browning – Williams

Williams Reserve Driver Luke Browning is preparing for his fifth FP1 appearance of the season, following outings in Barcelona, Austria, Italy and Mexico City.

The Briton, who also competes in Japan’s Super Formula championship, was awarded an additional practice opportunity after an electrical issue prevented him from completing any running in Barcelona. Browning returned to the cockpit in Mexico City, completing 33 laps as he continued to familiarise himself with the FW48 and the new regulations.

The 24-year-old will now replace Carlos Sainz at Interlagos, marking his final scheduled rookie outing of the campaign after stepping in for Alex Albon last time out.

Freddie Slater – Audi

Freddie Slater will be hoping for a smoother experience as he returns to Audi’s R26 following a disrupted first F1 practice appearance in Mexico City.

The 18-year-old, who became the first member of Audi’s Driver Development Programme earlier this year, saw his running compromised after a cooling fan was inadvertently left attached to his car, resulting in a €7,500 fine for the team.

After finishing runner-up in F3 this season, the Briton is preparing to step up to F2 with Invicta Racing in 2027.

He will replace Nico Hulkenberg in Brazil after driving Gabriel Bortoleto’s car in Mexico City.

Gabriele Mini – Alpine

Gabriele Mini will make his second consecutive FP1 appearance for Alpine after his official F1 weekend debut in Mexico City.

A member of the Alpine Academy since 2023, the Italian previously completed Testing of Previous Cars (TPC) running in July before stepping into Franco Colapinto’s A526 at the Autodromo Hermanos Rodriguez.

The 21-year-old finished P14, just over seven tenths behind Pierre Gasly, despite a Virtual Safety Car disrupting his final soft-tyre run.

Currently fourth in the F2 standings with two victories and seven further podiums, Mini will return to the cockpit at Interlagos, this time replacing Gasly.

Colton Herta – Cadillac

Colton Herta will make his sixth FP1 appearance of the season as the American continues his pursuit of the Super Licence points required to compete in F1.

The former IndyCar driver has been balancing his F2 campaign with test driver duties for Cadillac, completing practice outings in Barcelona, Hungary, Italy, Austin and Mexico City. Currently 19th in the F2 standings, Herta has impressed Cadillac during his F1 appearances and remains a potential candidate for a future race seat.

After falling short of the required mileage in Mexico City, the 26-year-old needs to complete at least 100 kilometres on Friday to secure his final Super Licence point.

He will replace Sergio Perez in Sao Paulo after stepping into Valtteri Bottas’ car last time out.

Rafael Camara – Haas

While the other rookies will hand their cars back after FP1, Rafael Camara is preparing for his full Formula 1 debut in front of his home crowd.

The 21-year-old Brazilian, who currently leads the F2 standings and has secured titles in Formula Regional and F3, was originally due to join Haas as a full-time driver in 2027.

However, his debut has been brought forward following the team confirmed Esteban Ocon would no longer compete for them, with reserve driver Ryo Hirakawa replacing the Frenchman in Mexico City and scoring a point on his F1 debut.

Hirakawa’s World Endurance Championship commitments have since opened the door for Camara, who impressed Haas during a TPC outing at Portimao in August.

A member of the Ferrari Driver Academy since 2021, Camara will partner Ollie Bearman for the entire weekend. He has never raced at Interlagos or driven the team’s 2026 challenger, but will have three practice sessions to get up to speed ahead of Qualifying.

Haas have yet to confirm who will occupy the seat for the remaining rounds of the season.

title: Alan Permane handed Racing Bulls Team Principal renewal
excerpt:
Alan Permane has signed a long-term contract extension that will see him remain Team Principal and Co-CEO Sporting of Racing Bulls through to the end of 2031.

Permane joined the team as Racing Director in January 2024 before being promoted to Team Principal in July 2025, following the departure of Laurent Mekies – who left to become the Team Principal of Red Bull Racing following the departure of Christian Horner.

Since then, Racing Bulls have claimed their first podium under the VCARB name at the 2025 Dutch Grand Prix and finished sixth in last year's Constructors’ Championship, matching the squad’s previous best result.

The team have continued to score points regularly in 2026 and remain in contention for fifth in the championship, which would represent their best-ever Constructors’ finish.

“I am immensely proud to be continuing this journey with VCARB,” said Permane. “We have the right people, the right culture and a clear sense of where we want to go, and I am excited to keep pushing together.”

Oliver Mintzlaff, Red Bull CEO of Corporate Projects and Investments, said the new deal would give Racing Bulls “stability and continuity” as the team look to build on their recent progress.

"Alan is doing a tremendous job, and the progress the team has made is a direct reflection of his experience, commitment and competitive mindset,” said Mintzlaff. “He brings clarity, composure, and a deep understanding of what it takes to perform in Formula One, while creating an environment where people can consistently deliver at their best.

“The results Visa Cash App Racing Bulls has achieved in recent seasons underline the strength of the team and the work being done throughout the organization. Alan has played a key role in that progress, and we are very pleased that he will continue to lead the team as we look to build on this momentum in the years ahead.

'I don’t know what else they want me to do' – Lawson elaborates on uncertainty around his F1 future

“Together with Peter Bayer as Co-CEO Commercial, Alan forms a strong and experienced leadership team. They complement each other exceptionally well, bringing different strengths and perspectives to the organization. I am delighted that we have this stability and continuity in place, providing a clear platform for the team’s future development and long-term ambitions.”

Permane has more than three decades of Formula 1 experience, including 34 years with ‘Team Enstone’ – most recently in their Alpine guise – where he held roles including Race Engineer, Chief Race Engineer and Sporting Director, and was part of championship-winning campaigns with Michael Schumacher in 1994 and 1995, and Fernando Alonso in 2005 and 2006.

title: All the stories that got the Sao Paulo paddock talking
excerpt:
Kimi Antonelli has barely had a moment to catch his breath since clinching the 2026 world title in the high-altitude surroundings of Mexico City’s Autodromo Hermanos Rodriguez – and the young Italian was still beaming when he touched down in Brazil for the final phase in what has been an action-packed triple header.

Antonelli’s title celebrations

Antonelli’s drive to P3 behind Ferrari’s Lewis Hamilton and Red Bull’s Max Verstappen last weekend – despite feeling the effects of illness and the pressure of sealing the deal – was enough to put the championship beyond mathematical doubt and spark a long line of emotional celebrations and press duties.

Those continued after Antonelli made the roughly nine-hour flight to Sao Paulo, where he spoke at a special press conference with Mercedes’ Title and Technical Partner Petronas on Wednesday, and reflected on what had happened some 72 hours earlier.

title: Norris wary of new McLaren upgrades in Sao Paulo
excerpt:
McLaren will introduce new upgrades for the Sao Paulo Grand Prix this weekend, with Lando Norris stating he wants "to believe that we can still make improvements" to this year's car.

Norris has endured a difficult campaign as the reigning World Champion, an accolade he lost last weekend as Kimi Antonelli became Formula 1's youngest title winner.

After a difficult start to the season, Norris and McLaren claimed back-to-back wins during the summer, but have since struggled to fight for victory, primarily down to a car which is difficult to push to the limit for both the Briton and team mate Oscar Piastri.

Speaking on Thursday's media day in Brazil, Norris was hopeful new upgrades would help make the car more drivable, but warned it could also make the problem worse.

"I did my preparation earlier and clicked on the screen where we see the results of every session, and it’s easy because my name was at the top of all of them," said Norris, who won in Sao Paulo 12 months ago.

"So it was a nice reminder. Obviously, at this point last year, I just took control of the championship, and then I had a very successful weekend. So it was a very good one and obviously a big confidence booster at the time.

"But I always enjoy it here, and I think after Mexico, we want to be hopeful. We want to believe that we can still make improvements. We’ve got some small things to add to the car this weekend, so we hope that can move us in a better direction.

"I don’t know if it’s going to make it easier to drive. It could even make it harder to drive, but hopefully the performance takes a step forward. So maybe then you can adjust some things to potentially make it more consistent.

"But the team are working very, very hard on trying to improve this year’s car to make it not just quicker, but also a car that is more compliant with what a driver needs when trying to extract the limit.

"There’s always been very good potential, but getting it out of the car is not always very easy. So hopefully we can make some small changes this weekend."

title: Antonelli reveals 'incredible' messages after becoming champion
excerpt:
Kimi Antonelli admits that "the support has been incredible" since he became Formula 1's youngest World Champion, and has revealed his favourite messages ahead of the Sao Paulo Grand Prix.

Antonelli secured the 2026 title in his sophomore season last weekend after finishing third in the Mexico City Grand Prix, becoming World Champion at the age of just 20.

The Mercedes driver beat the record for the youngest champion previously held by Sebastian Vettel, and revealed on Thursday's media day in Brazil that a video from the four-time World Champion had been a personal favourite amongst many.

"It’s been an amazing two days, but I still haven’t had enough time to realise and digest what has just happened. Definitely, I’m very happy. It still feels surreal," said Antonelli.

"I’ve received so many nice messages, so much support, and I’ve had a lot of videos from my hometown celebrating. The support has been incredible. It’s really hard to pick one single moment or one single action that impressed me the most because they were all super nice.

"But I think the message from Seb was very nice. It was very deep, with a lot of meaning behind it and a lot of advice for the future. So that was very nice.

"But I also got a lot from other drivers, from Max, Lewis, Charles. Everyone was super nice. Lando was super nice to me as well. So I’m very happy and grateful to see so much respect and support.

"I’ve also had the chance to recharge and enjoy a couple of days doing some really nice activities, especially spending time with the Senna family. That was truly incredible and something that I will remember forever.

"So yes, it’s been very demanding in some ways, but I’ve had the time and the chance to relax and recharge. It was also very nice to see so much excitement and support around me."

Mercedes can still claim the teams' title this weekend in Brazil and Antonelli admits beyond that, he is looking to just enjoy the remaining races while fighting for the wins.

"The goal coming here is to win. It’s a track that I love, and the fans are amazing here. So I’m really looking forward to it," said Antonelli.

"The goal is to have a great weekend, but also to enjoy the rest of the season. Obviously, we’ve still got races to go, races where we want to do well. So I’m looking forward to it. It’s definitely a really cool place to start everything again after clinching the title and to get a win."

title: Piastri leads F1 community in tributes to Alan Jones
excerpt:
Drivers, teams and other members of the Formula 1 community have paid tribute to 1980 World Champion Alan Jones, who passed away at the age of 80 on Thursday.

The Australian racer will forever have a place in the history books as he led the charge in taking Williams to their first drivers’ and constructors’ titles alongside team mate Carlos Reutemann, with Jones clinching five Grand Prix victories over a dramatic season.

His collaboration with team boss Sir Frank Williams and technical chief Sir Patrick Head was instrumental in the outfit’s rise to becoming a powerhouse in F1, making a significant impact on both Williams’ and Australia’s place in motorsport.

Speaking ahead of the Sao Paulo Grand Prix, Jones’ compatriot Oscar Piastri said: “I think it's obviously a very sad day. A life that should be very well celebrated. I think [he was] a guy that obviously had a lot of success on the racetrack and was Australia’s most recent World Champion.

“But I think also the person he was, you know, a very straightforward person, straight to the point. On a personal level as well, he often had nice things to say about me, which was nice.

“I’ve had the honour to drive his World Championship-winning car as well, so [it was] very cool to be able to experience that and connect with him in some kind of way. A sad day, but a day that should celebrate a great life.

“Obviously he was a long, long time before me, and I never had much interaction with Alan. But I think in a lot of ways, he kind of embodied the Australian spirit – very tough, saying it how it is, saying what he thinks, and I think that’s probably the biggest thing.

“Anyone that’s won a World Championship in F1 has clearly achieved it through talent, hard work, all kinds of other things, so I think that probably says enough.”

Current Williams drivers Carlos Sainz and Alex Albon also marked Jones’ achievements as he remains a key part of the team’s legacy.

“Very sad news, given also that Alan was such a strong figure for Williams in our history,” Sainz reflected. “Being our first winner, our first champion, it’s obviously a big loss for the team, as he’s done so much for us. He will be missed. All my best regards to the family and close friends.”

Albon added: “Deeply saddening. Alan was a legend to Williams, and I think he’s brought so much success to the team, and moved the team forwards in many ways. A really sad loss for everyone, but of course especially for us.”

While those on the 2026 grid weren’t around to watch Jones compete in F1, McLaren CEO Zak Brown shared a personal memory of the driver’s prowess and how important he was in encouraging his lasting passion for motorsport.

Another figure who has honoured Jones’ memory was fellow Williams champion Damon Hill, who followed in his footsteps to win the 1996 title, becoming the sixth of seven drivers to taste glory with the British team.

Formula 1 President and CEO Stefano Domenicali said: “I am deeply saddened by the passing of Alan Jones, a true great of our sport and an extraordinary racer. Alan was a formidable competitor, a natural leader and an icon who inspired generations of fans, particularly in his beloved Australia.

“His place in Formula 1 history is assured, not least for bringing Williams their first Drivers’ and Constructors’ World Championships in 1980, a defining moment for the team and our sport. But beyond his achievements on track, Alan will be remembered for his character, his passion and the lasting mark he left on Formula 1.

“He will be greatly missed by the entire Formula 1 family. On behalf of Formula 1, I send my heartfelt condolences to his family and loved ones. Our thoughts are with them at this very sad time.”

title: Why Russell had ‘to get out’ after Antonelli’s title win
excerpt:
George Russell has confessed that he needed “to just get out” after a frustrating race in Mexico City, combined with seeing team mate Kimi Antonelli secure the Drivers’ Championship, left him to rue his “rubbish season”.

With a P3 finish, the Italian secured the title for good as it’s now mathematically impossible for any other driver to surpass his 380 points in the remaining rounds, making him the youngest champion in F1 history.

Although Antonelli’s triumph was highly likely heading into the Mexico City Grand Prix, Russell at least had a chance of victory after he missed out on pole position by just 0.009s to Ferrari’s Lewis Hamilton.

However, his hopes of challenging for the lead disappeared when a deployment issue impacted his start, which caused him to drop down the order before making contact with Isack Hadjar. Adding to his woes, he received a 10-second time penalty for the incident and ultimately wound up sixth.

“I was extremely disappointed Sunday night, more from the fact of missing out on a great result from something again outside of my control, and that was just a really tough pill to swallow,” Russell explained in Sao Paulo.

“This season it’s been ‘tough moment, pick yourself back up, tough moment, pick yourself back up’. And I think, as an individual, I’ve continued to have that resilience of being able to always pick myself back up, and it kind of just got to the point in me where I was like, ‘I need to just get out of here’, because it’s just been relentless what’s happened this year.

“It’s been tough. I’m here, four days later, ready to go again. And I think for any individual, or sportsperson, or businessperson, you never have every year of your life that goes the way you want.

“We all have problems we deal with. We have good days, bad days, good years, bad years. I think it’s important to not let that define you – you’ve just got to come back stronger, and that’s what we’re here to do.”

The overwhelming day also saw Russell skip his post-race media duties and take time away from the track, with the numerous reliability problems he’s endured this season still fresh on his mind.

From a power unit failure whilst leading the Canadian Grand Prix to repeated straight line speed deployment troubles, the Briton’s title ambitions were partly limited by the performance of his W17.

He admitted: “I don’t think I’ve ever had this many setbacks in my career. I went through – after the race with my engineer – the season race by race, and we realised we had six races this season with no issues, and 14 races where we’ve had an issue of some sort.

“To give perspective, in the years gone by, we would maybe have two races where there were issues, or I think in 2023 we had four races where we had issues. This season we’ve had 14 races.

“I’ve always sort of picked myself back up. As much as I love talking to [the media] after the race, I didn’t really fancy it on this occasion, so I was like, ‘I’m going to just get out of here and go for a nice dinner and think about something other than the rubbish season we’ve had’.”

title: Damon Hill offers Ferrari simple Hamilton-Leclerc solution: 'Ends all debate'
excerpt:
Damon Hill believes Ferrari has a straightforward way out of its Lewis Hamilton-Charles Leclerc mess: make the seven-time F1 champion the team's clear number one driver.

The debate around the Scuderia flared up again after the Mexico City Grand Prix, where Hamilton started from pole position but had to fight hard to keep Charles Leclerc behind him on the opening lap.

It went wrong at Turn 4, where both drivers ran off the track. Leclerc then took the lead by cutting across the circuit, leaving Hamilton to settle for third place behind Max Verstappen.

Leclerc was later handed a five-second penalty for the move, but Verstappen used the pit-stop window to seize the lead himself.

It meant Hamilton missed out on a win that had been within his grasp. He made clear afterwards that he wants rules put in place at Ferrari to stop such clashes happening again, bearing in mind what also happened at Monza and Zandvoort recently.

Hill, the 1996 F1 champion, feels Ferrari can put a stop to it.

Hill, via X, wrote: "Here is where I stand on the Lewis v Charles debate, and I made this point in my commentary on Sunday in Mexico.

"Make Lewis #1 Ferrari driver. Sort it out. Make it clear. Ends all debate. Lewis will deliver for Ferrari. If they back him 100%"

title: Oliver Bearman handed apology after 'misjudged' accident: 'Gave him a shove'
excerpt:
Nico Hülkenberg has revealed he apologised to Oliver Bearman after the pair's coming together on the opening lap of the Lap 47 restart at the Mexico City Grand Prix ended the Haas driver's race.

The Audi driver tapped the rear of Bearman's car as the field bunched up following the restart, sending the Briton into a spin from which he could not recover, sustaining damage that forced him out of the race.

Hülkenberg was handed a 10-second time penalty for the clash, a punishment that dropped him from a potential points finish to P16 in the final classification.

The two had been scrapping just outside the top ten when the incident occurred, meaning both had their afternoons wrecked by the clash.

Speaking to media, including RacingNews365, Hülkenberg explained the circumstances that led to the contact.

"Yeah, it was just obviously racing Lap 1 [of the restart]; many cars bunched up together, and I was obviously racing another car, braking into Turn 4," the Audi driver explained.

"In the wake of all these cars, I just lost downforce and had a bit of a rear lock. I couldn't stop the car in time, and then gave him that shove."

Hülkenberg: 'I misjudged that one a little bit'

The German revealed he went straight to Bearman to clear the air once his media duties were done: "I went after the [media] pen and straight away to see him and the team, and apologised to them."

Hülkenberg was clear in accepting responsibility for the clash, despite insisting there was no malice behind it.

"It was not intentional, and it was not ideal, obviously, to finish his race like that. But yeah, it's on me," the 39-year-old acknowledged.

"But it's part of racing; in a way, these things can easily happen, and obviously I misjudged that one a little bit."

title: Lando Norris reveals upgrade hope amid unwanted McLaren five-race streak
excerpt:
Lando Norris has revealed he is hoping McLaren's latest upgrade package can put the team back into podium contention this weekend, as the Woking-based squad continues its longest barren run of the season.

Norris and McLaren have gone five races without a podium finish, a drought stretching back to Azerbaijan, with the Briton's results in that run ranging from fourth to a retirement in Baku.

McLaren has introduced a revised front wing, a modified rear wing and new floor components for the São Paulo Grand Prix, aimed at recovering aerodynamic performance that has slipped behind rivals Red Bull, Ferrari and Mercedes in recent months.

The update also doubles as an early test for a front-wing concept destined for next year's car, according to the team.

But Norris has cautioned that the small package carries risk as well as reward, warning it could make the already tricky MCL40 harder to drive on the limit.

Lando Norris eyeing podium 'as soon as possible'

Asked whether the new parts could push McLaren back into the fight for podiums, Norris told select media, including RacingNews365, that he was uncertain but encouraged by recent underlying pace.

"I hope so. I don't know. I certainly feel like the last few weekends, the pace has not been too bad on Sundays," he said.

"So I feel like if things had gone just a little bit better, talking small amounts, we certainly could have had better results. And I'm hoping that the upgrades and some of the things we have this weekend can maybe just shift us a little bit more in this direction.

"I certainly don't expect to go out and win races all of a sudden, but the last few weekends we've certainly not been miles away. We certainly have some weaknesses in the car, and just the drivability, the difficulty of driving it, is certainly one of the biggest factors at the minute, but the potential has been there.

"So, I hope if it just puts us a little bit further forward in qualifying, we just have a little bit better of a chance in the race. And, of course, I would like to be back on the podium as soon as possible."

title: McLaren unleash latest F1 upgrades in rare Sao Paulo GP situation
excerpt:
McLaren are all alone when it comes to introducing upgrades this weekend!

McLaren will be the only team to bring new parts to this weekend's São Paulo Grand Prix, with the FIA's official car submission document confirming a fresh front wing, rear wing, beam wing and floor for the Woking-based squad at Interlagos.

In a very rare situation, no other constructor on the grid has declared an upgrade package for round 20, according to the FIA filing, leaving McLaren's development push notably isolated this late in the campaign.

The new front wing is understood to focus on flow conditioning across its elements, aimed at sharpening the airflow reaching the floor and sidepod bodywork.

The revised rear wing and beam wing have reportedly been designed to generate downforce more efficiently while improving how the rear-end elements work together aerodynamically.

The floor update, meanwhile, is said to target more stable underfloor airflow management, addressing balance inconsistencies that have cropped up in recent rounds.

McLaren upgrades with eye on 2027 development

Beyond its immediate performance aims, the front wing concept introduced at Interlagos reportedly doubles as an early track test of aerodynamic ideas McLaren is exploring for its 2027 challenger, under the sport's incoming regulation cycle.

Neither McLaren personnel nor outside technical analysts have put a specific lap-time gain on the package, with evaluation instead said to be centred on downforce efficiency rather than a stated numerical target.

Interlagos itself offers a useful proving ground, blending low-drag straights with a demanding, bumpy middle sector that tests underfloor sensitivity more severely than most circuits on the calendar.

The hope of Lando Norris is that the upgrade will push McLaren back towards Mercedes, Ferrari and Red Bull, following a five-race run without a podium.

title: Kimi Antonelli issues health update after fighting Mexican illness
excerpt:
Kimi Antonelli has given an update on his health after battling illness throughout the Mexico City Grand Prix weekend, revealing he feels much improved but is still not back to full fitness.

The newly-crowned world champion struggled with a virus in Mexico, a weekend in which he nonetheless finished third to seal the title at the age of 20.

Antonelli missed media day in Mexico City due to recovering from the illness, with Cadillac's Valtteri Bottas and Sergio Perez both also being unwell across the most recent round.

Speaking on media day in Brazil, Antonelli explained that the celebrations which followed appear to have helped shift the illness.

Asked about his condition, the Mercedes driver told select media including RacingNews365: "I feel better. I think all the viruses left my body after the celebration on Sunday night.

"I think they left my body, so I definitely feel better. But, no, I think I'm still recovering a bit, but I feel better than I did in Mexico. Definitely in Mexico, I wasn't feeling well all weekend, so I definitely feel better on that side.

"Not 100 per cent, but I think that's a bit the same for everyone. Triple-headers are usually quite demanding. But definitely on track, now I will not be as tense.

"Now that the championship is done, I think I will be able to enjoy driving even more. But the important thing is going to be not to relax too much."

Kimi Antonelli focus switches to 2027 preparation

Antonelli's title-winning weekend was followed almost immediately by a visit to Ayrton Senna's family estate in Tatuí, where he sat in the Brazilian legend's 1986 Lotus 98T and met members of the Senna family, including Bruno, Bianca and Paula Senna.

The whirlwind schedule, the Italian admitted, has left him little chance to properly take stock of becoming Formula 1's youngest ever world champion.

"Well, for sure, I would have liked a bit more time to just digest what happened," Antonelli said.

"I've had such a crazy sequence of events in these days. I won the championship, then went to the Sennas and spent time with the Senna family, which was already another incredible event.

"So, definitely, I would have liked a bit more time to just sit down and reflect and realise what happened. But I'm actually very excited to be here, and I think it's a good opportunity for me, first of all, to try to finish the season on a high."

He added that his focus has already shifted beyond the remaining rounds of 2026.

"But I also feel like my 2027 preparation starts now, so it's going to be important to finish the season well and strongly, in order to have the confidence going into 2027," added the world champion.

"So, yeah, I feel like my preparation for 2027 starts now, and then once the season is over, I get a few days to enjoy everything else."

title: Aston Martin take 'unhappy' stance after 'insufficient' fix to 'abnormal' Honda issue
excerpt:
Both Aston Martin cars dropped out of the Mexico City Grand Prix early on with Honda power unit issues.

Aston Martin has explained how its options to complete the Mexico City Grand Prix were "insufficient" as its Honda power unit suffered an "abnormal" issue.

Both Fernando Alonso and Lance Stroll retired within five laps of the race at the Autodromo Hermanos Rodriguez, which is 2,285m above sea level and where the air is around 20% thinner than at sea level.

This means the turbo is required to work harder to perform - a task made harder in 2026 with the removal of the MGU-H from the power units, which induces turbo lag.

Alonso was forced to stop his car in qualifying on what he felt was shaping up to be a strong weekend, with the race-ending faults found to be in the cooling circuits of the power units.

Honda described the issues as stemming from "special circumstances" in Mexico, including double warm-up laps for the tyres and the formation lap, with the ERS cooling circuits being placed under undue strain - thus leading to MGU-K failures.

The cars ultimately retired with water pressure problems, one too high and one too low, as chief trackside officer Mike Krack explained the reality of the situation the team found itself in.

"I think nobody was happy. We've had a lot of DNFs, and we had another double DNF, so nobody can be happy, and I think it is the same for Honda," Krack told media, including RacingNews365, as he confirmed the team had realised before Sunday's race that completing the 71-lap distance was going to be tricky.

"I think you need to be realistic when you prepare for the possibilities of the race.

"There are a few, so we discussed the different levels of escalation and the possibilities.

"The first one is obviously free air, but then you have gear usage, and you can turn down the power, so there are many options we discussed, but we did not get that far.

"There is a list of options, but we quickly realised they were insufficient, and there is nothing you can do."

[Article continues below]

© XPB Images

Honda's response

Offering Honda's take on the situation, chief engineer Shintaro Orihara explained how the power unit had been caught out by the special circumstances of Mexico City's altitude and thinner air, with countermeasures being deployed at Interlagos.

"I can't explain in detail, but I can give you some more ideas, Orihara explained.

"We have the laps to the grid, which is a unique point, and a tyre preparation lap. We had laps in free practice, but in a different situation, so in those special circumstances, our engine behaved a little abnormally, or not as expected.

"Then we had some stress on the ERS cooling circuits and then had a failure on the MGU-K that happened in qualifying in special circumstances and that was because of the high altitude in Mexico.

"Brazil is not the same as Mexico, but still on the high-altitude side, so we will bring some countermeasures for this event, not only on the hardware side but also the software side to improve our robustness.

"The problem did not directly link to traffic; it doesn't help PU operation, but it was not directly linked to the problem."

Addressing Alonso's comments about the weekend and "hard lessons" being learned after failing at the "moment of truth", Orihara confirmed that investigations were underway at Sakura.

"It was also hard for Honda, and I understand the frustration," he said.

"In special circumstances, there is a lack of robustness [in the engine], so we can always learn something from this type of problem, and we will bring the old problem to the factory [and ask]: 'How can we prevent these things from happening again in the future?'

"At this moment, the factory is focusing on the 2027 power unit, but we can apply this experience to improve the robustness of next year's engine."

title: Isack Hadjar cautious over major Red Bull problem fix: 'I'd be lying if I said yes'
excerpt:
Isack Hadjar has sounded a note of caution over whether Red Bull can replicate the strong race starts it finally produced in Mexico City, as the team heads to Interlagos still searching for consistency off the line.

Red Bull's starts had been a persistent issue throughout the season, with unpredictable clutch delivery repeatedly costing both Hadjar and Max Verstappen positions at the first corner.

The problem was at its most costly in Austin, where Hadjar dropped away from third on the grid after what was described as an uncontrollable clutch overdelivery at the moment of getaway.

No hardware fix was introduced before Mexico, yet the Milton Keynes-based team's launches improved markedly there, with Verstappen converted fifth on the grid into a strong win.

Despite the exceptional starts for both cars in Mexico, Hadjar is not ready to call the issue solved.

Asked if Red Bull's strong starts in Mexico can be repeated, the Frenchman told select media, including RacingNews365: "I'd be lying if I said yes, because, I mean, I also don't want to say it was a fluke, because we worked hard on it from Austin, and then we achieved it in Mexico. So, lots of hard work.

"Now the goal is to replicate it, find out why it worked that well, and keep it that way until the end of the year. And next year, take an even further step."

Isack Hadjar confident form is 'going to click'

That hedge reflects a wider theme in Hadjar's recent weekends, as Red Bull's RB22 has been capable of winning races in the hands of his team-mate.

But Hadjar's own results have not matched the car's potential, with mechanical and electronic gremlins, from a gearbox failure in Singapore to a late battery issue that cost him a likely podium in Malaysia, repeatedly disrupting his Sundays.

Discussing now having a race-winning car at his disposal, Hadjar explained: "That's what makes it more frustrating for me right now.

"The last couple of races, I couldn't even be in the top five. I mean, except for Malaysia, it's always been something happening on Sunday.

"But, yeah, it's going to click. It's just a matter of time, and on my side, I think the pace has been decent. So I just want to keep pushing, and here anything can happen with the conditions, so stay very, very sharp."

title: FIA recognises mind-blowing world record as 500 km/h barrier smashed
excerpt:
This is absolutely crazy what was achieved in Abu Dhabi!

The YANGWANG U9 Xtreme has become the first production car to break the 500 km/h barrier, hitting a top speed of 503.17 km/h during a high-speed run in Abu Dhabi.

The record run took place on 1 November on the Sheikh Khalifa Bin Zayed International Road in the United Arab Emirates' Al Dhafra Region, with the FIA officially recognising the speed.

It beats the previous mark of 496.22 km/h, which the same car set in Germany in September 2025.

The Abu Dhabi run has also landed two Guinness World Records, for the highest speed achieved by a production car and by an electric production car in a single-direction run.

German racing driver Marc Basseng was behind the wheel for the record, just as he was when the U9 Xtreme set its previous benchmark at the ATP Papenburg proving ground.

The milestone caps a rapid development programme by YANGWANG, the luxury electric arm of Chinese manufacturer BYD, since the U9 project launched in 2024.

The original U9 reached 309 km/h in testing in China that January, before touching 391.94 km/h at Papenburg in October 2024. The Xtreme version then jumped to 472.41 km/h in August 2025 and 496.22 km/h a month later, meaning the Abu Dhabi figure represents a further gain of 6.95 km/h.

Article continues below...

How the record was broken

The Abu Dhabi attempt ran over two days, with local authorities and the FIA closing a 10 km stretch of road that included a seven-kilometre straight for the runs.

Two initial attempts on 31 October topped out at 490 km/h. Engineers then reworked the car's aerodynamics, suspension settings and tyre pressures overnight to sharpen stability, before two further runs followed on 1 November. The second of those delivered the record-breaking 503.17 km/h.

The U9 Xtreme is powered by four independent electric motors producing a combined output of more than 3,000 PS, built around a 1,200-volt electrical architecture.

It also runs an advanced torque-vectoring system and bespoke high-performance tyres developed with Giti Tire, alongside an active suspension system and battery and thermal-management tech built to cope with the demands of high-speed electric running.

The car already holds the production EV lap record at the Nürburgring Nordschleife, having lapped the circuit in 6 minutes 59.157 seconds.

With the FIA's recognition of the 503.17 km/h run now confirmed, the YANGWANG U9 Xtreme stands as proof of how far all-electric production cars have come in outright performance terms.

title: F1 boss gives cautious 'at this stage' verdict on season-ending Middle East races
excerpt:
MotoGP is in Qatar this weekend, will F1 be there in three weeks?

Formula 1 still expects to close out the 2026 campaign in Qatar and Abu Dhabi, but Stefano Domenicali has stopped short of guaranteeing it, citing ongoing tensions in the Middle East.

The F1 CEO's cautious choice of words came as Liberty Media published its third-quarter financial results, which showed the sport's revenue stabilising after a turbulent first half of the year.

A reshuffled calendar and the cancellation of the Saudi Arabian round had triggered a 38 percent revenue drop in the three months to June 30 compared with the same period in 2025.

But the picture has since levelled out, with revenue for the nine months to September 30 reaching $2.496 billion, just $2 million down on the equivalent period last year despite one less race being held and the Bahrain Grand Prix taking place in Malaysia.

The third quarter alone brought a 28 percent year-on-year revenue jump to $1.115 billion, helped by one extra race compared to the same window in 2025.

Operating income rose from $433 million to $450 million over the first nine months, though adjusted OIBDA slipped five percent to $649 million.

Grand Prix

Qatar GP

Stefano Domenicali 'still expects' 23-race 2026 calendar

Domenicali told the Q3 earnings call that he still expects the 2026 calendar to run to 23 races, one fewer than in 2025, despite the Qatar and Abu Dhabi Grands Prix facing disruption from conflict in the region.

"I'm proud to say that we again demonstrated F1's ability to solve challenges by successfully staging the Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia, and the event was a resounding success, reflecting the resilience of our business model and the incredible ability of our teams and partners to find creative solutions to ensure we can go racing," Domenicali said during the Liberty Media Q3 call.

"I'd also note that the disruption we experienced in the Middle East this year does not change our long-term regional strategy and ongoing partnership with our promoters.

"This year we currently remain scheduled to complete our calendar this season and at this stage continue to plan to finish the season in Qatar and Abu Dhabi."

title: Carlos Sainz reveals 'hardcore' Charles Leclerc fans 'insulting me' was tougher than racing him
excerpt:
Carlos Sainz has revealed the toughest part of his Ferrari partnership with Charles Leclerc was not the racing itself, but the abuse dished out by his former team-mate's most hardcore supporters.

Sainz's comments land at an awkward moment for Ferrari, with Lewis Hamilton and Leclerc now the ones generating headlines for the wrong reasons.

The pair collided at Turn 4 in Mexico City, with Leclerc handed a five-second penalty. They were also involved in a separate incident at Monza where Leclerc squeezed Hamilton wide at the first chicane. Tension later flared at Zandvoort, when Leclerc was reluctant to follow instructions to let Hamilton through.

Team principal Frederic Vasseur has since accused both drivers of showing a lack of respect towards the team following the Mexico clash, while Hamilton has pointed to the absence of clear rules of engagement within the garage.

As far as Sainz is concerned, the Williams driver can understand the perspective that when fighting at the front, with a win in your sights, it is hard for a driver to not fight for the opportunity.

Sainz, teammates with Leclerc at Ferrari from 2021 to 2024 before being ousted for Hamilton, in speaking to media, including RacingNews365, said: "Honestly, I have relatively good memories of my time with Charles and the fights we had.

"It is true that when you're fighting for wins, there's always more pressure, more things on the line, so you naturally become a bit more selfish than when you are fighting in the midfield for a P8 or a P9.

"It's more difficult to follow exactly the ideal situation that the team would like you to follow, because there's a win on the line.

"There were wins on the line back then, but I think I always respected Charles. He always respected me. We never had contact or anything like this. We just had strong fights. I think you remember Monza, Vegas. There were plenty of hot moments during the year."

[Article continues below]

Sainz made clear that the sharpest edge of that era came not from wheel-to-wheel racing but from the partisan reaction it generated, in particular from the Leclerc fans.

"I think what was more difficult was that the PR and the fan base were really ignited back then, and it was very polarised between Charles and me, and I remember suffering a bit from the very hardcore fans of Charles insulting me or wishing me bad," said Sainz.

"Maybe some Italian media were also saying that I was not being enough of a number two when I needed to be, and vice versa when Charles had to do it.

"So it's more the pressure surrounding Ferrari that involves Ferrari than the actual issues that I had with Charles, which were always resolved that same night when we called each other with a cooler head, and we always managed to find the solution and the way forward."

title: George Russell eyes Lewis Hamilton heroics as Brazil grid penalty confirmed
excerpt:
George Russell will take a five-place grid penalty at this weekend's São Paulo Grand Prix after Mercedes opted to change the internal combustion engine on his car.

The change is a standard ICE replacement, drawn from the car's seasonal hardware pool and built to match its previously homologated specification.

An ICE change of this kind involves replacing the V6 block along with its core mechanical components, including the cylinder heads, pistons, crankshaft and valvetrain, while other elements such as the turbocharger or motor generator units can be retained separately.

Exceeding a driver's seasonal allocation of any power unit element automatically triggers a grid penalty under F1's cost-containment rules.

Russell addressed the penalty in a Mercedes Instagram story, pointing to the timing of the change.

"I had to take a grid penalty at some point from Singapore until the end of the season," said Russell.

"We felt like this was a good place to take it. Lewis [Hamilton] had a big grid penalty here a number of years ago and did pretty well. Five places doesn't seem that bad, and we'll try and come back through."

Lewis Hamilton took a far heavier hit at Interlagos in 2021, dropping to tenth on the grid for Mercedes before fighting through the field to beat Max Verstappen on lap 59 and win the race.

Russell's penalty is considerably smaller, but the Brit is clearly hoping for a similar story at the same venue.

title: Red Bull make key decision as senior Racing Bulls figure handed contract extension
excerpt:
Alan Permane has signed a new long-term contract that will keep him in charge of Racing Bulls as team principal and co-CEO sporting through to the end of 2031.

Permane joined the Faenza-based outfit as racing director in January 2024, working alongside Laurent Mekies before being promoted to team principal in July 2025.

Since that promotion, the team has claimed its first podium under the Racing Bulls name, at last year's Dutch Grand Prix, and matched its best-ever constructors' championship finish with sixth place in 2025.

This season has brought further progress, with the team establishing itself as a regular points scorer and still fighting for fifth in the constructors' standings, a result that would represent its best finish in the championship.

Oliver Mintzlaff, CEO Ccorporate projects and investments at Red Bull, credited Permane's influence on the team's upward trajectory.

"Alan is doing a tremendous job, and the progress the team has made is a direct reflection of his experience, commitment and competitive mindset," Mintzlaff said.

"He brings clarity, composure, and a deep understanding of what it takes to perform in Formula One, while creating an environment where people can consistently deliver at their best.

"The results Racing Bulls has achieved in recent seasons underline the strength of the team and the work being done throughout the organisation. Alan has played a key role in that progress, and we are very pleased that he will continue to lead the team as we look to build on this momentum in the years ahead.

"Together with Peter Bayer as Co-CEO commercial, Alan forms a strong and experienced leadership team. They complement each other exceptionally well, bringing different strengths and perspectives to the organisation. I am delighted that we have this stability and continuity in place, providing a clear platform for the team's future development and long-term ambitions."

Permane brings more than three decades of Formula 1 experience to the role, having started his career at Benetton.

He spent 34 years with the team that became Enstone, working as race engineer, chief race engineer and then sporting director, and won world titles alongside Michael Schumacher and Fernando Alonso during that spell.

Permane himself expressed pride at extending his stay with the team, thanking Red Bull for their backing.

"I am immensely proud to be continuing this journey with VCARB, and I would like to thank everyone at Red Bull for the trust and support they have given me," Permane said.

"What makes this team special is the shared spirit of everyone; trackside, in Faenza and in Milton Keynes, and it is a privilege to lead such a talented and committed group every day.

"Fighting for fifth in the championship is something we should all be very proud of, but it is the result of years of hard work from a lot of people, and we are not done yet. We have the right people, the right culture and a clear sense of where we want to go, and I am excited to keep pushing together."

title: Lando Norris explains 'unbelievable honour' after losing F1 champion privilege
excerpt:
Lando Norris has spoken of his "honour" and pride at being able to carry the #1 in 2026 as the reigning world champion.

Norris will lose the right to carry the #1 for the 2027 season as Kimi Antonelli has succeeded him as champion, with the Italian now having the opportunity to carry the only driver number not freely available and reserved for the champion.

However, Antonelli has confirmed that he will not run the #1 in 2027, preferring to stick with his personal driver number of #12.

Since driver numbers were standardised in 1974, and personal numbers were introduced in 2014, only Lewis Hamilton has not run the #1 as reigning world champion who defended their title, preferring to carry the #44 during his title-winning years at Mercedes. He did run the #1 in 2009 at McLaren.

Reflecting on his year carrying the #1, Norris, the 35th champion, who is to revert to his personal number of #4 in 2027, spoke of his pride at handing the number over to Antonelli, even if the 36th champion won't be using it.

"I'm happy to see it go to someone who deserves it, and Kimi has done an incredible job this season, so I'm very happy that it will go, let's say, towards his hands, whether he uses it or not. I don't know," Norris told media, including RacingNews365, of the #1.

"He has plenty of years, a lot more years than I do, to try and get it again in his future, so of course it's been more about how it makes you feel than anything.

"I don't think physically it really does anything, but the mentality side, the feeling of going out there, knowing that I'm a world champion, knowing that I'm on not a long list, but a list of unbelievable drivers and drivers that I looked up to when I was a child, the honour of seeing my name alongside Max [Verstappen] and Lewis [Hamilton] and so many of the people that have made the sport such a success, that makes you feel special.

"That makes you feel things that nothing else really in the world makes you feel. So that's something I'm very, very proud of."

[Article continues below]

Feeling of the number 1

Norris then expanded further on the honour of carrying the #1, and how he and team reflected on the journey to be able to hold the number.

"I think it's something that we all, as a team, are very, very proud of, so it's not only the personal achievement of doing it, but it's also the achievement of the success with my team, the people that I worked with to achieve it," he continued.

"Every time we can see the number one on the car, it just is a nice reminder for us. I don't think it changes anything. It doesn't make you think you're better than you are. It doesn't make you feel like anything you deserve anything more.

"I think we understand that as a team, but it makes you proud of the achievements and the hard work that you put in through your whole life.

"So it's more of a positive reminder than anything else. So of course, it is a shame to see it go, but at the same time, I'm happy to see it go to someone who deserves it."

title: George Russell opens up on ‘exhaustion’ after being constantly ‘kicked to the ground’
excerpt:
George Russell has explained his "exhaustion" at constantly having to "pick myself back up" after his crushing F1 season.

After Kimi Antonelli sealed the drivers' title in Mexico City last weekend, Russell congratulated his champion team-mate before quickly leaving the circuit and not being part of the team celebrations.

He then issued an emotional statement "from the heart" after his season, which has been derailed by various technical gripes with the power unit, and being forced to adapt his driving style to the new engines.

Russell has finished on the podium once since the Italian GP, his victory in Azerbaijan, as power unit penalties, deployment issues, or even power unit failures have cost him dearly, as he has now slipped to fourth in the drivers' championship.

Reflecting on the mental toll the 2026 season has had, Russell spoke of the tough positions he has found himself in.

"I probably just feel a bit exhausted this season of constantly picking myself back up,” Russell explained to media, including RacingNews365.

"When you get kicked to the ground, you pick yourself back up, and then you get kicked down again; you pick yourself back up.

"I was hoping to do that maybe twice in the season, not every other weekend.

"When you get to this point of the season, you’re away from home for three weeks in a row, and you have another race like what happened in Mexico, where a chance of victory, a chance of the podium, just disappears totally outside of your control. It’s tough to deal with."

title: Exclusive: Lewis Hamilton-Charles Leclerc Ferrari feud branded 'a good problem to have'
excerpt:
Guenther Steiner has waded into Ferrari's latest F1 driver drama, insisting the team principal Fred Vasseur is dealing with "a good problem to have" after Lewis Hamilton and Charles Leclerc clashed again in Mexico City on Sunday.

Hamilton and Leclerc ran off circuit together at Turn 4 on the opening lap of the Mexico City Grand Prix as they fought for the lead. It culminated in Leclerc cutting across the grass at Turn 5 to emerge ahead, while Hamilton dropped behind Max Verstappen.

The four-time F1 champion went on to win the race after Leclerc was handed a five-second penalty for gaining a lasting advantage off-track. It marked the latest flashpoint between the Ferrari teammates in 2026, following incidents at Zandvoort and on the opening lap at Monza.

Vasseur has previously rejected calls for formal written rules of engagement between the two drivers, preferring informal team principles over a rigid hierarchy.

Steiner, the former Haas team principal, believes that approach is the correct one given the personalities involved.

Speaking about the situation, Steiner said it was not a case of Ferrari facing a crisis, but rather the kind of dilemma most teams would envy.

[Article continues below]

Steiner - 'Hamilton was frustrated'

"It's a good problem to have," said Steiner. "Now, you could say there's never a good problem.

"But you've two very good drivers. Obviously, how do you manage them? But I've been in similar positions. You cannot manage the drivers when they're out there racing.

"I'm not saying that what Charles did was 100 per cent right, but it was also not completely wrong. He's a race car driver. He wants to push as well. In the end, it ended badly again. That's the unfortunate thing.

"But to find a solution there, I don't envy Fred because you've got two champions, two very good drivers, and obviously they both want to win.

"Obviously, what happened didn't help them because they didn't win the race, but what can you do?

"Lewis was frustrated, but I don't think that Charles backed down. He said, 'Okay, I cannot just sit there waiting to be second. That doesn't work for a race car driver.

"It's not easy to manage, but it's better to have this problem than a guy who is not performing, one of the two."

Steiner also backed Vasseur personally to handle the fallout, pointing to the Frenchman's track record of standing firm with strong-willed drivers.

Asked about Vasseur's approach, Steiner said: "In the end you want the team to perform, but then you need everything to perform.

"At least they didn't run into each other. They were smart enough not to do that, so it's not easy. But as I said, it's a good problem to have, not a bad one."
